title: Norway moves to ban facial recognition on AI smart glasses in public spaces
subtitle: Digitalisation Minister Karianne Tung opens the government's expert-group review and urges retailers to pause Meta Ray-Ban sales while legal clarity catches up.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Norway's government has opened an expert-group review that is expected to produce temporary rules on AI-enabled smart glasses, with a specific target: banning facial recognition features on camera-equipped eyewear in public spaces. Digitalisation Minister Karianne Tung told Norwegian press this week that the review will deliver preliminary recommendations before year-end and that the Norwegian Consumer Council has already urged retailers to pause sales of Meta Ray-Ban glasses until the legal framework is clear. The push is one of the first national-level moves in Europe to specifically target the glasses form factor rather than facial recognition generally.

The mechanism Tung objects to is not any one Meta feature — it is the combination. Smart glasses pair an always-aimed camera, a microphone, and an on-device AI model that can describe or search what it sees in near real time. The result is a device that can covertly capture bystanders and, with the right software layered on top, match their faces to names. Norwegian prosecutors and the Consumer Council have both flagged this as a specific risk to women and to anyone in a space where they have a reasonable expectation of not being identified — public transit, pharmacies, courthouses, shelters.

The move puts pressure on the broader European debate. The EU AI Act prohibits remote real-time biometric identification in public spaces for law enforcement with narrow exceptions, but consumer-grade smart glasses sit in a different corner of the law — they are a product, not a public-sector deployment. Several European countries have raised similar concerns about Meta's glasses over the past year, and Norway's expert group may become the de facto template for how to regulate a device that was designed to be invisible. Meta has not yet responded publicly to the pause request.

A takeaway for learners: the hardest regulatory problems in AI are rarely about the models themselves — they're about where models get deployed and who else is in the room. A camera that lives on someone's face changes the implicit consent model that other privacy rules were built around. If you want to understand why 'AI regulation' is harder than 'software regulation,' this is the clearest live example. Watch what Norway's expert group concludes; it will shape what gets banned, labeled, or required to beep when it records.
